I think this is the wrong approach. A larger proton collider is not likely to tell us much. The reason is that protons are composed of several interior particles that share the proton's kinetic energy. Only two of those interior particles collide, and the random sharing of energy makes it hard to tell what the actual collision energy is.

At high energies, we need to collide electrons or positrons, which contain no particles inside themselves. The entire collision energy goes into the reaction. The date is very clean and easy to interpret, so the statistical confidence is much better. The Large Electron-Positron (LEP) collider proposal is important.

We also desperately need to build a muon collider. Muons are traditionally thought to merely be heavy versions of electrons, but we have little data on this assumption. The data we do have says they are not just heavy electrons but have unique mysteries all their own. We need muon experiments of all kinds.

We also need to prioritize wake field accelerators, which were recently invented. They use lasers to reach ultra-high energies that circular colliders can never hope to reach. If we want to experiment at nigh-magical energies, wake field machines are the only game in town.
